The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.

Monday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZN

Tuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.

A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.

There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.

#1281. The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

By the time a baby is born, its brain has lost large numbers of neurons with genetic abnormalities.Credit: Getty

Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously tidies up by purging itself of a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons, according to a painstaking analysis of more than 2,300 nerve cells.

We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person

We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person

The analysis, published in Nature1 on 28 October, found that more than one-quarter of the sampled neurons from the brains of human fetuses had either gained or lost several segments of their chromosomes. By contrast, only about 6% of neurons from the brains of babies after birth had such abnormalities. “It suggests that the neurons that survive may be the ones that have kept the most intact genomes during development,” says Christos Proukakis, a neurologist at University College London, who was not involved in the study.

The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says Diane Shao, a paediatric neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts and first author on the paper.

Learning more about this process could be key to understanding neurological conditions that often appear in childhood, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy.

Studies in mice2 have suggested that, during early development, mammals eliminate many brain cells by activating a molecular programme that leads to the cells’ deaths. Shao and her colleagues analysed human brain development by studying the brains of deceased individuals ranging from fetuses at 14 weeks of gestation to nonagenarians. The team focused on neurons in the cerebral cortex, a region of the brain responsible for memory, learning and consciousness, among other functions.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

The team analysed the genomes of individual neurons to look for those that had either lost or gained some chromosomal segments, a phenomenon called copy number variation. The analysis revealed that a stunning number of cells with widespread copy number variation were present during fetal development. There were so many that Shao and her colleagues spent years trying to work out whether the results were real. But even after repeating the experiment using a different single-cell sequencing method, the results were similar.

After birth, however, the proportion of these abnormal neurons dropped by more than fourfold, suggesting that they had been culled during development.

How does the brain know which neurons are normal and which are not? One possible clue, says Shao, is that those brain cells with high levels of copy number variation also tended to show abnormal activity of genes involved in forming connections, or synapses, with other neurons.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03444-x

Shao, D. D. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11190-3 (2026).

Article  Google Scholar

Peterson, S. E. et al. J. Neurosci. 32, 16213–16222 (2012).

#1280. Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

Eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

“We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta said. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

“The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

“I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO

Yet Madueke provided the crucial contribution, driving a right-footed shot towards goal which took a heavy deflection off Forest defender Jair Cunha to beat Matz Sels.

Madueke has struggled for consistency and minutes since his £52m move from Chelsea, so this felt like a big moment for the winger.

“If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke said. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We showed grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”

Forest’s problems at home are increasing and Oliver Glasner is now the club’s fifth manager in a year to experience such problems. His team have now gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters. They have only recorded two home wins in the league over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

They did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

Liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Murillo had Forest’s best opportunity two minutes into injury time after cutting inside the penalty area but could not find the top corner.

"That was magic!" What a goal this would have been from Murillo?! 😩 https://t.co/D07lB7hN47

Another defeat will only add to their concerns and Glasner needs to quickly find a solution or face another relegation battle.

It does not promise to get easier immediately, either, with Manchester City, Chelsea and Brighton up next in the league at home, but there were encouraging signs here, despite the club sitting in the bottom three.

Glasner said: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

“It feels unfair but I don’t want to be complaining as we are the only ones who can change it.

“It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

“We are playing better right now but we also concede how competitive the Premier League is because every mistake you get punished.”

We knew the margins would be really small. They are extremely well coached and organised. The longer the game goes on they gain more belief. We had to be so patient - and clinical when we got the chance. The way they were defending, they were more comfortable. But we have players with different qualities and can adapt to what the game is delivering.

We have another three big chances that should be goals. That is the difference, you have to be clinical. If we keep generating them, they will come.

Let’s enjoy the win, because it was a very tough one. And then, on Wednesday, we have an incredible game against Bayern Munich away [in the Champions League].

When you see their goal it’s deflected otherwise, it’s straight to the gloves of Matz Sels. You have periods in football where you feel everything going against you and then there are periods when things are on your side.

Now it is how we deal with the situation and react as a team and just how we can change this is by staying positive, sticking together and working hard.

And having this coolness, not to worry too much because I can see good performances and not good results. The results will come if the performances stay good.

Noni [Madueke], Jurrien [Timber], Mikel [Merino] was brilliant when he came on and Viktor [Gyokeres] really changed the game - all of them did and that’s what we need. Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that’s the difference.

Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn’t have a shot on target and that’s something we discussed. We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it’s in.

Great reaction [after scoring goal], to have the will to defend a really open and difficult and stressful situation.

We knew it would be a tough game, it always is against Arsenal. They have a good team. But we feel we can change the result, maybe a draw, maybe a win. Now we have to put it in the past and focus on the next match.

We have a good manager and I think we are still getting his ideas. We changed everything in our system this season. It is difficult but after three or four months we keep improving and I think we are close to reaching our best.

If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd so we know that we’re going to start some and finish some and for me it’s the same mentality every time I just want to create or score.

Amazing feeling [to score] but I feel better about the win.

We have elite players, all 20-something players are elite and of the highest level. Great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench you’re ready to have an impact.

32 - Since Mikel Arteta became Arsenal manager in December 2019, they have had the joint-most 1-0 wins in the Premier League of any side (32, level with Everton). Stereotype. https://t.co/nD7C3j7Xjw

Arsenal dig out a very ugly victory, and one they probably did not warrant. A draw would have been the fairest outcome from a game that was low on quality, but Arsenal’s bench makes a difference again with Noni Madueke scoring the winning goal. Forest can take positives from their performance, primarily the solidity of their defending and a more threatening Delap performance.

Forest with another late moment of danger! Delap peeled in behind the Arsenal defence, and he was found by a glorious pass, but Konsa made a fantastic last-ditch challenge to surely preserve the points from Arsenal.

What a goal that would have been from Murillo! The burly defender did so well to skip between Konsa and Saka, before sending Rice the wrong way in the box with a roll of the studs. Murillo tired for the curler into the top corner with his weaker right foot, and he was not far away. Great effort.

"That was magic!" What a goal this would have been from Murillo?! 😩 https://t.co/D07lB7hN47

Arsenal have a throw in the Forest half after some grafting by Gyokeres and there are just three added minutes to play.

Was that Forest’s chance?! Quick thinking from Liam Delap on the halfway line caught Arsenal out, launching a quick throw into the path of Hudson-Odoi with Timber ahead of the ball. Hudson-Odoi carried the ball to the edge of the box and picked out Wood with a pass, but the big striker wanted too much time and Rice recovered to block.

Anything can happen when there is a one-goal margin, but Arsenal have been in complete control since scoring. Forest have lost some of their structure as they chase the game and they are more open as a result. Merino wins a free-kick, and then Gabriel ushers the ball out for a throw in.

Forest cling on by their fingernails with Arsenal flooding forward, but Merino’s pass to Saka in the box was underhit. Chris Wood and Hudson-Odoi are now on for Forest as they chase an equaliser. Cunha and McAtee the Forest players to depart.

Arsenal have kept a grip of the game since the goal, Gyokeres with some willing running to ensure the game remains in Forest’s half.

The Arsenal winger was helped by a deflection, but after Forest’s defence beckoned him to cut inside on his right foot he took up the invitation. It was a clean strike from Madueke, but the flick off Cunha’s thigh was crucial and the ball flew past Sels into the roof of the net.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Saka floats in a teasing cross which bounces through to Sels, but that was a better Arsenal delivery. One or two signs that Timber, and his combination with Saka and Odegaard, might be the route to a goal.

Odegaard with a week free-kick from a good crossing position after Saka won a foul, before Raya’s long ball towards Gyokeres is too strong and Forest have a goal kick. Arsenal still to muster a shot on target from 73 per cent possession.

Ndoye are Dominguez are the Forest players coming off in a double change, replaced by Kalimuendo and Sangare. Forest will be worth a point if the game continues this way.

Declan Rice with a shank out for a throw when he was looking for Saka. Kalimuendo is ready to come for Forest, so Glasner is introducing another forward.

Good chance for Rice but he blasts over! Arsenal’s best move of the game with Saka, Odegaard and Timber working as a triangle to get in behind the Forest defence, and Timber’s pull-back was accurate. Rice was always leaning back though as he tried to sweep the ball into the far corner.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO

Delap with a tame shot from distance, before Timber instigates a more dangerous Arsenal attack with a reverse pass into Odegaard. The ball is worked to Madueke and his deflected cross is headed away. Saka wants a throw but the linesman has other ideas. Still no goal despite more endeavour in this half.

Arsenal building some pressure, and they have another corner. Arteta signalling that he wants to make the change before the corner is taken and here come the changes: White for Timber, Havertz for Gyokeres and Merino on for Bruno Guimaraes.

Gabriel meets Rice’s delivery, but he fails to direct his header on target.

Excellent defending from Gabriel up against Ndoye in the right channel, but it was another promising moment for Forest in this second half. Madueke then isolates his man one-on-one, and wins another corner.

Timber, Merino and Gyokeres are all ready to come on for Arsenal.

The game is see-sawing, Arsenal have a corner after Calafiori fed Madueke down the left and his cross was blocked. Sels punches away, and then Odegaard loses some patience and tries to find Calafiori with a pass that is not on.

Saka and Rice lose duels when fishing for fouls and Forest have another corner. Arsenal’s performance level has certainly not improved since half-time.

Arsenal clear, but Odegaard blocks a cross and Forest win a second corner in quick succession. Excellent goalkeeping from Raya to claim, and he bowls the ball forward quickly, but Forest snuff out the danger against Madueke.

The first half was an attack against defence session for long periods but Arsenal know they are in an arm wrestle now. Forest far more aggressive, and the crowd are more involved. But that could open up avenues of space. White with a really poor pass towards Saka which is astray.

Arsenal have a corner of their own after breaking from Raya’s gloves. Much more open game so far.

Forest deal with Saka’s delivery, and there was a very brief VAR check for a handball penalty. Nothing doing.

Madueke looking dangerous, receiving a Gabriel ball over the top and dashing inside but his shot was blocked.

The winger then tried to make amends, but he gave away a free-kick at the expense of a booking.

Delap’s shot from a tight angle is then deflected wide. Forest corner, from which Murillo’s header loops into Raya’s gloves. Forest showing more attacking ambition.

Liam Delap is producing a very decent centre-forward performance.

The £50m record signing is proving a real threat with his power and running.

Madueke and Rice not one the same wavelength, before Delap does well to win a shoulder to shoulder with Gabriel only to slice his cross behind for an Arsenal goal kick. Sums up the lack of attacking quality in the game.

Forest have another free-kick in a shooting position after Havertz is penalised for blocking a long shot with his hand. McAtee’s effort from the free-kick is scooped miles over the bar.

Both teams looking livelier in the early exchanges of the half, but Forest’s counter-attack was the more dangerous, with Liam Delap doing well to hold on to the ball and whipping a cross into the box that was just ahead of Williams.

Noni Madueke replaces Eberechi Eze, so a more natural wide player on his stronger foot on Arsenal’s left flank.

Frustrating first half for Arsenal and Mikel Arteta will be demanding more from his attacking players.

Arsenal have not registered a shot on target so far and their delivery from set-pieces has been poor.

Forest look relatively comfortable and had the best chance of the half with a shot from Dan Ndoye which was saved by David Raya.

Are we heading for a hat-trick of 0-0 draws at the City Ground between these two teams?

A very uneventful 45 minutes which has been played at the pace of a pre-season game at times. Similarities with the last two fixtures between these teams at the City Ground, and Arsenal’s games against Leeds and Lille this week. They put their foot on the pedal after half-time in both games, and they need to do the same here.

Guimaraes is off the pitch, and there will be more than two minutes added now as a result of his treatment. Forest win a corner, but Havertz heads away at the near post.

Just the two minutes of added time to play.

Liam Delap wins a free-kick in a shooting position for Forest after Arsenal were caught with numbers forward. Big moment for the home team, this. Calafiori was caught on the ball again, he has not had the best of games.

Williams and McAtee are over the free keek, which is around 25 yards out, left of centre.

Williams blasts the ball into Bruno Guimaraes, who goes down and stays down after taking the shot flush in the face.

More incisive from Arsenal, with Rice punching the ball into Odegaard and then on to Havertz but the angle was always against him and the German could only shoot into the side-netting. Forest have defended very well, overall. Although they have been deep for the most part, they have jumped and pushed out at the right times to stop Arsenal accessing the box.

Glasner and Arteta dish out some instruction while there is a stoppage in play to deal with a hand in the face that troubled Schlager. Can either side find a breakthrough before the break?

David Raya claimed that Forest corner with ease and the game has now resumed its pattern. Forest retreating into their shape, and Arsenal passing in front of them. Schlager penalised for a foul on Saka, the home fans not happy with the decision, I think because Saka was going away from goal.

Rice clips in a menacing delivery, but Havertz skewed his header wide from seven or eight yards. Good chance, Arsenal’s best so far.

More Arsenal probing but the small details are letting them down: Eze’s return to Odegaard forced his team-mate to check, and then Odegaard’s touch was heavy after a wall pass from Guimaraes.

Delap does well to make a nuisance of himself at the other end, and his long-range shot deflects behind for a corner.

Strong from Konsa to win the ball, drive out of defence and win a foul. Rice with a well-weighted scoop over the Forest defence for the run of Ben White, but he skewed his cross behind for a goal kick.

Arsenal with another corner. No doubt they have been the game’s dominant force when it comes to possession and territory, but there has been a lack of cutting edge so far. Saka goes for the near post again but Forest deal with it. The home crowd groan at Sels for not releasing the ball quickly in search of a break.

Arsenal work the ball across their midfield with Guimaraes, Rice and Odegaard all involved, and a dangerous Saka cross is headed behind for a corner.

Scramble! The near-post flick on caused chaos and Konsa’s goal-bound backheel was blocked, but the ball would not quite drop for Ben White to score a tap-in.

After two successive goalless draws here between the two clubs, this is following a similar script so far.

It’s a very tight affair with Arsenal enjoying more of the possession but Forest seemingly happy with that and content to them on the break.

Bruno Guimaraes has made a bright start for the visitors.

Forest’s best attacking moment of the game and it comes from an Arsenal mistake.

Calafiori just had to play a five-yard pass back to Gabriel but scuffed it, and Munoz pounced. Running at the Arsenal penalty area, Munoz’s cross was deflected to the back post and the ball found it’s way to Ndoye. Decent reverse shot through legs, but Raya had it covered and tipped around the post.

From the corner, Forest are penalised for a foul.

Arsenal continue to have Forest penned in their own half, very difficult for the home team to play through the midfield or over Konsa and Gabriel so far.

Saka produces his first successful dribble to beat Williams, and the left wing-back trips him at the expense of a free-kick and a booking. Rice’s delivery from the right was uncharacteristically poor.

Munoz tries to drag Forest up the pitch to apply some pressure on Arsenal but he is penalised for a shirt pull on Gabriel. The atmosphere sounds pretty sleepy, a result of some tepid Arsenal possession and Forest’s bad home record.

Forest making sure they have numbers around Saka whenever Arsenal funnel attacks down their right, which is almost always their preferred side.

Neat from Guimaraes in midfield to turn and find Saka with some earlier service, and Sels tips his cross away from danger.

Delap and Ndoye waiting for a slip-up or counter-attack but they are feeding on scraps at the moment. Arsenal yet to carve out a proper chance, though.

It’s already pretty clear that one of the key duels today will be between Gabriel and Liam Delap.

Forest’s record signing Delap has already let Gabriel know he’s in the game with his physicality.

Cute pass from Bruno Guimaraes to break the Forest midfield line and find Odegaard, but strangely the Arsenal captain could not sort his feet out to control the ball and back a clean pass. Then Williams defends well against Saka from an Arsenal attacking transition.

Pretty subdued start from Forest. The crowd’s spirits were raised there by Delap chasing down Konsa who had the deal with the sun his eyes, but the Forest striker pushed him in the back.

Arsenal enjoying all of the possession so far, and most of it has come in Forest’s half. One or two players on Arsenal’s right/Forest’s left struggling with the low evening sun. Havertz did get in behind but his cross into the middle was too strong.

Arsenal get the game under way, and play short from kick-off.

There will be a degree of pressure on birthday boy James McAtee today to make an impression.

With Morgan Gibbs-White injured, McAtee is likely to take the No 10 position and continue his redemption arc.

McAtee has been revitalised since the arrival of Oliver Glasner and this is a big afternoon for the former England under 21 international.

In honour of nine-year-old Forest fan James Kerry, who died earlier this month of cancer.

We'll wear black armbands this afternoon, as we join our hosts in remembering nine-year-old Nottingham Forest supporter, James Kerry, who passed away earlier this month following a brave battle with cancer. Rest in peace, James ❤️ https://t.co/YFIXnCfJJX

Surely we cannot have another 0-0 in this fixture? Looking at the talent in Arsenal’s front third, and the fact they are playing their two most offensive full-backs, this might be more open than assummed.

Arsenal can cut Manchester City’s lead to three points with a win today but does it all matter?

Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict is threatening to run into next year and this title race feels fake and damaged.

It is a sham of a season with the prospect of asterisks all over the Premier League campaign.

Arsenal can only carry on as normal as they defend their title but this is an unsatisfactory mess.

The margins are really small and it’s a team and a manager that we know really well, extraordinary manager, really well organised.

They are dangerous in many areas, a very well set-up team and you need to be very tight, very neat, very efficient in everything that you do. You have to insist and insist, and then there’s a lot of volume of actions.

[On coming from behind] Yes, and it’s part of the game, your capacity when something doesn’t go as planned to react and still win the game, and we know the challenge that we have here. In the last two years, we haven’t been able to win here and that’s an opportunity as well to show what we are made of.

Another reason Arsenal will be feeling confident today is Forest’s abysmal home form in the Premier League.

It may surprise neutrals outside of Nottingham but results at the City Ground have been poor for some time.

Indeed, it is just two league wins in 11 months in front of their own supporters which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Before this game, Forest’s head coach Oliver Glasner said: “We have to change it. I spoke to one or two experienced lads who know Forest better than I do and talked about the situation. But if you always talk about the problem it makes it bigger and bigger.

“We haven’t scored a goal at home yet or won a game at home, and that is what we have to change.”

Trips to the City Ground have seldom been easy for Mikel Arteta, with two successive 0-0 draws in the Premier League.

An FA Cup defeat in Jan 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparked a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

Yet Arsenal have secured two wins in a row since that defeat at Brighton, without being truly at their fluent best, and will be confident against a Forest team without injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White.

Dominguez and Schlager are the preferred midfield pair in the 3-4-2-1 with Sangare on the bench. McAtee and Ndoye will support Liam Delap in attack. Much attacking responsibility on Munoz at right wing-back, who also has the cavalier Calafiori on his side of the pitch, which could prove fireworks.

Things started with a phone call with Nicolas Jover, then a meeting with Arteta and now he splits his time between Argentina and London. Find out more about Arsenal’s mystery man and his methods here.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

#1279. Premier League Power Rankings: Manchester United falling fast; Tottenham Hotspur, Bournemouth rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight games into a campaign, patterns are supposed to emerge as teams begin to lock into midseason form. This season of the Premier League is no exception, except the pattern is a new one – expect chaos until further notice.

Several teams are experiencing a regression to the mean after rocky starts to the season, evidenced by the weekend's most notable games. Aston Villa are surging up the table after a 2-1 win over Manchester City, Bournemouth defeated Manchester United in style with a 3-0 triumph at Old Trafford and Tottenham Hotspur have gone from zero wins to two in a week, a 2-0 win at Chelsea their most impressive performance in months. Others are also putting their early season results behind them, but it feels like they are crashing back down to earth – Brentford were held to a 1-1 draw at Hull City, while Ipswich Town were unimpressive in a 1-1 draw against Nottingham Forest.

A fascinating theme is beginning to emerge along the way. It feels like there are more midtable teams than usual, even if some sit as high as seventh (someone has to, after all). Then there are those that seem like relegation contenders but are several spots above the drop zone because, somehow, there are that many teams worse than them. There's a frenetic feeling to the Premier League table and, by extension, the latest edition of power rankings but the show must go on.

Here's how each Premier League team is looking after the latest round of games.

Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton was not glamorous but the Gunners won't care. They're level on points with Manchester City and well-positioned to compete for the title, much as they have been all season.

Manchester City's short-lived grip on first place is gone after their defeat to Aston Villa, one that raises questions about their ability to go the distance in Enzo Maresca's first season in charge.

Liverpool are slowly but steadily figuring things out with Andoni Iraola at the helm, a 2-0 win over Brighton and Hove Albion their most impressive result yet. A top-four spot feels like a realistic aim for this season, even if they are not the finished product just yet.

Fabian Hurzeler's side played a fairly even game with Liverpool, so their stock should not drop too much but the Reds did map out a plan to neutralize their attack-minded tendencies, which might be something opponents borrow from in the coming weeks and months.

This is where the extreme midtable energy of the Premier League comes in – Chelsea were deeply unimpressive against Spurs, unconvincing at almost every turn. Most teams in England's top flight, though, are worse off so the Blues hang onto fifth for now but they will be worth keeping an eye on.

Between a 3-0 win over AC Milan in the UEFA Europa League and their triumph at Old Trafford, it has been a fun week to be a Bournemouth fan. Those wins are a sign that things are finally clicking – they might be 13th in the league but they rank third on expected goal differential, a signal that things were always trending in the right direction.

Aston Villa's slow start is officially a thing of the past, Unai Emery's side smartly outmaneuvering City to prove just that. They are officially a team on the rise.

Leeds United's unstylish but effective consistency means they continue to hang out in the top half of the table but playing even against an unimpressive Sunderland side is not the kind of thing a team earns plaudits for.

There's no reason Brentford should not target a top-half finish but much like Leeds above them, an even game against relegation contenders Hull City is not indicative of the team's overall qualities.

Manchester United really have their hearts set on scaling down the table as fast as they can, don't they? The Red Devils should be better than this but their mistake-prone nature continues to be costly.

A win over Coventry City is one thing but a victory at Chelsea is another. More specifically, it's the kind of thing that ensured Spurs would dig themselves out of their early season hole and perhaps sets them up for some more normal results in the short-term.

There is no shame in losing to the reigning champions but Everton did not make much of a dent in the match, the Toffees seemingly resigned to being permanent residents of the middle of the Premier League's table for the foreseeable future.

For all their faults, Fulham have done well enough to pick up the points expected of them, the latest coming in a win over Coventry City. Barely cracking 0.5 expected goals along the way, though, is not something to write home about.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the other shoe will drop for Hull City but it hasn't yet, especially after picking up a well-earned point against Brentford.

Add Nottingham Forest to the list of anomalies this season, sitting firmly in the relegation zone despite ranking fifth in the league on expected goal differential. Case in point – they tallied 2.29 expected goals to Ipswich's 0.46 but tied 1-1 anyway. Until they solve that problem, they are doomed to less-than-ideal spots on the table.

Ipswich were lucky to pick up a point against Forest but the early season success is a thing of the past for them, too.

Eighth-place Newcastle United seem to be riding their luck – they rank 19th in the league on expected goal differential – but creating a five-point cushion above the drop zone by way of a win over Crystal Palace counts for something.

Sunderland will value the point they picked up against Leeds but they are in the midst of an unexciting season, which is hardly a position of strength for a team in desperate need of points.

Palace will take some solace from the fact that they outplayed Newcastle but in their case, the results actually reflect their form.

Coventry were neck-and-neck with Fulham on expected goals in defeat but considering the Cottagers put up a paltry number, there's not much the newly promoted side can brag about.

#1277. 'Players run through brick walls for him': How Scott Parker will fix West Ham - Mark Noble's helping hand, why insiders believe he can shed defensive style... and where it all went wrong for 'distant, dour' Nuno Espirito Santo

Published: 12:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EDT, 3 November 2026

For a club that prides itself on playing the 'West Ham Way', it has long been impossible to decipher quite what that means these days.

Managers have come and gone with no one able to tell you what their West Ham team embodies. What was the identity under Julen Lopetegui? What was it under Graham Potter? And what, after more than a year in charge, was it under Nuno Espirito Santo? If anything, the longer it went on under Nuno, the more unclear it became.

There had long been concerns in the West Ham dressing room, and boardroom, about Nuno’s confusing tactics, unforgiving man-management and humdrum training sessions. Club insiders described him as distant.

Few can forget the time he played his full backs on the wrong side in a damaging defeat by Brentford and then sent his team out against Leeds with no recognised forward and Andy Irving in midfield.

It was little surprise to see Callum Wilson, the former Hammers striker who started on the bench in those games, liking the club’s Instagram post confirming Nuno had been sacked.

Nor to see current jettisoned midfielder Edson Alvarez do the same when he can’t get into the side despite EFL record signing Arne Engels and Divine Mukasa being overrun every week. And especially not to see the wife of goalkeeper Alphonse Areola, now playing second fiddle to Mads Hermansen, posting an Instagram story to the tune of So Long, Farewell from The Sound of Music.

There had long been concerns in the West Ham dressing room, and boardroom, about Nuno Espirito Santo’s tactics, man-management and training sessions

In Nuno's stead, West Ham have turned to former midfielder Scott Parker to get them out of the Championship

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse, another who was bombed out under Nuno, could barely conceal his glee when asked last month after his Southampton side's win at the London Stadium whether it felt even better to get one over a manager who didn’t want you. ‘I’m not gonna lie,' he said, 'of course it does.’

Nuno’s fate is not expected to be mourned for long. West Ham’s supporters had already made their own views clear.

Spurred on by the travelling West Brom fans at the London Stadium on Saturday with their hearty rendition of ’You’re getting sacked in the morning’, the few Hammers left at the end of their 3-1 home defeat joined in.

Three days later, they got their wish. ‘Following a thorough review of the start to the Championship season, the board of directors believe a change is necessary at this time to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track,’ read the club statement.

Those expectations are to earn instant automatic promotion, considering West Ham have the most expensive squad in the division and kept hold of Jarrod Bowen after relegation. But they are eighth following those back-to-back defeats by Southampton and West Brom.

It was a surprise to many that Nuno kept his job after relegation. David Sullivan, the former majority shareholder, wanted to sack Nuno in the summer but his influence in the boardroom was fading amid the BBC Panorama expose into historic allegations about his behaviour, which he denies, that saw him stand down as joint-chair.

Daniel Kretinsky, now the man who makes the decisions, wanted to keep the ship steady but has realised a change is needed after their unimpressive start. He made the decision after a crunch meeting this week.

And, so, for their fourth permanent manager since they enjoyed European glory under David Moyes, the Hammers will turn to one of their own former players in Scott Parker, out of work since leaving Burnley in April.

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse (centre), who was bombed out under Nuno, could barely conceal his glee after his Southampton side's win at the London Stadium

The club's expectations are to earn instant automatic promotion. But they are eighth following back-to-back defeats by Southampton and West Brom

The club hope he could even be in charge for the Cardiff game on Wednesday night. They held talks with Parker in the summer and are believed to have done so again last week following the Southampton defeat.

Insiders say the club is acting with more ‘normality’ these days under the leadership of new chief executive Karim Virani, a stark change from the madcap chaos of recent years, and the appointment of Parker, a manager with a track record of getting teams promoted, feels like another step in that direction.

Parker has won three promotions with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley, with the last coming after racking up 100 points in 2024-25.

And, perhaps even more importantly at a time when the club are still searching for an identity, the 46-year-old – who was named Hammer of the Year three times in a row from 2009 to 2011 – knows what it means to represent West Ham. ‘He knows the West Ham ethos,’ as one senior club source told me this morning.

It’s expected that Hammers legend Mark Noble, currently sporting director and in interim charge, will form part of Parker’s staff. The fans, at least, will have figures in the dugout they can feel connected to.

Parker’s first job after taking over will be instilling a resilience that typified his Burnley team. West Ham boast the best attack in the Championship with 33 goals, helped by pumping six past Wrexham and Lincoln, but they have the leakiest defence of any of its top 11 teams.

Eight of their 18 goals conceded have come inside the first 20 minutes and, so far this term, they have failed to win when conceding the first goal.

By contrast, Parker's sides have kept a clean sheet in nearly half of his Championship matches. Burnley kept 30 in their 2024-25 promotion campaign, conceding 16 times in 46 matches and never more than once in a game. West Ham have mustered four clean sheets in their 13 games thus far and have already let in 18.

The 46-year-old - who was named Hammer of the Year three times in a row from 2009 to 2011 - knows what it means to represent West Ham

He will get a helping hand from former team-mate Mark Noble (left), who is now sporting director

Parker is arguably the safest pair of hands West Ham could have placed their promotion hopes in. Those hoping to be freed from the turgid football of Nuno, however, may still be left disappointed.

Parker’s sides do have an identity but it’s one based firmly on being hard to beat. Those who followed Burnley under him say that if they scored even once, they knew they would likely win. ‘Dour but effective,’ was how one Burnley source put it.

Even though they ended the 2024-25 season as the third-highest scorers in the Championship, they ranked only 10th for number of shots and their expected goals (xG). Eight other teams had more touches in the opposition box.

For all the grumbles over his style, Parker’s players loved him. ‘They would run through brick walls for him,’ said one Burnley source. An unusual flurry of long, heartfelt messages from his players followed the decision to part ways.

Those players who had their noses put out of joint by Nuno have a chance to reignite their West Ham careers.

Areola won the player of the season award at Fulham after Parker brought him to the club on loan from Paris Saint-Germain. Noble previously told talkSPORT how much he ‘always respected and liked’ Alvarez as a midfielder.

There’s still a hope among senior figures that having better players at his disposal will allow Parker to play a more attractive style than during his Burnley days. Many who follow the Clarets credit him with being able to build such a resilient team after losing a host of his key players at the end of the transfer window.

The issue, of course, is what happens should Parker get West Ham back up. For all his brilliance at getting teams out of the Championship, his record at keeping them in the Premier League is equally dismal.

Alphonse Areola won the player of the season award at Fulham after Parker brought him to the club on loan from Paris Saint-Germain

Parker was sacked after just four games at Bournemouth in the 2022-23 season

Fulham and Burnley came straight back down, the latter after spending more than £100million in the summer, and he was sacked by Bournemouth just four games in after a 9-0 defeat by Liverpool and complaints his squad was ‘under-equipped’.

Parker has won 55 per cent of his matches as manager in the Championship but only 15 per cent of them in the Premier League. His points per game plummets from 1.95 in the second tier to 0.7 in the top flight.

West Ham and their supporters may well harbour reservations over how they might fare in the Premier League under Parker but, right now, are in no position to think that far ahead. They need to get there first and, more than a quarter of the way through the season, have shown little to suggest they will.

Forget the carnival of free-flowing football for now. After putting up with a circus for so long, a little sense of order might be West Ham’s way back.

#1276. Why Bruno Fernandes got a second chance after missing penalty against Roma

Manchester United midfielder Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty in a home Champions League match against Roma, but was given a second chance after Bryan Cristante encroached into the penalty area before the kick.

Gianluca Mancini caused the penalty early in the second half, with Roma leading 2-0, after fouling Matheus Cunha.

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Feyenoord vs. Inter on the Liveblog.

Manchester United star Bruno Fernandes stepped up from the spot but missed his first chance, with Roma’s third-choice goalkeeper Devis Vasquez saving the low-driven shot to his right.

Referee Jesus Gil Manzano, however, ordered a retake after VAR showed Cristante encroached into the penalty area before Bruno Fernandes struck the ball.

Cristante was the first to get to the rebound after Vasquez’s save, so the referee’s decision, as suggested by VAR, was inevitable.

Bruno Fernandes, a former Novara, Sampdoria and Udinese midfielder, didn’t miss the second chance. He once again kicked the ball to Vasquez’s right, but this time closer to the top corner, while the Roma keeper dived the opposite way.

Vasquez is playing his first competitive match for Roma, as Milan Svilar has been out for weeks and second-choice keeper Pierluigi Gollini had back problems on the morning of the game.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

The water cycle is global, yet its accounting is not. Rain, rivers and underground water cross borders freely, but water use is reported by country. The budget for the world’s total usage is therefore only as reliable as the weakest report. When a country cannot measure usage, its water is lost from global accounting — and with it, any claim to a fair share.

#1274. Who's to blame for Manchester United's decline? Ranking the biggest culprits

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's happened again. Another season, another Manchester United crisis. No longer does the end of daylight savings time herald the harsh winter ahead. Instead, it is the boos that ring around Old Trafford as the United faithful turn their ire on the same owners, the same executives and the same players, well aware it will be a different coach that pays the price.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth was remarkable only for the sheer unremarkability of it. In the 74 years after their first meeting in the 1949 FA Cup third round, Bournemouth won three games against Manchester United. In the last two years they have won three games: all at Old Trafford, all 3-0. Freddie Kruger is treading the boards at the Theatre of Dreams.

Although maybe that analogy is not quite apt. After all, the one positive that you could say about a Krugerian nightmare is that it tends to be a one-and-done situation. No such luck if you happen to be a Manchester United supporter. Could any of them now believe that sacking Michael Carrick would fix anything about this club? They've tried the Eddie Howe-esque Premier League mainstay, the relentless winner a la Antonio Conte, the graduate of the Ralf Rangnick pressing academy in the mold of Julian Nagelsmann. Their shortlist only needs an ex-Ajax coach to sweep the quadrants of post-Sir Alex Ferguson ineptitude. Fred Grim to Manchester United? Well, doesn't that sound about right?

This is a club suffering under profound mismanagement, the sort that no one individual can marshal on their own. So there's plenty of blame to spread around. Let's start doing so, in reverse order of course. Gotta keep you on the page as long as we can. Build some suspense. Who might be top, you wonder? Well you probably know. But you know most every AAA movie is going to end with the hero triumphant. The joy is in the journey to the inevitable end point.

Now look, the soon to be former Manchester United manager is not without his faults, as Bruno Fernandes so robustly articulated after the 4-1 defeat in Como. There have been some very weird technical decisions here this season and a head coach with a scintilla of authority probably could have got this team to stop taking so many shots from outside the box. And yet did anyone at Manchester United genuinely think they'd unearthed the next great coach when they threw him the salvage our season post-Ruben Amorim job?

That Carrick did so much more than that, guiding United to Champions League qualification through a third-placed finish, spoke to his ability to keep things simple. He retained what had worked from his predecessor, tidied up some of the complexities of the formation and rode Bruno Fernandes' player of the season form as far as he could go. It is not his fault that United have not kicked on since. What had the 45 year old achieved in three seasons at Middlesbrough that suggested a coach who would do much more than what most coaches do, get a team to perform at or around its talent level?

Maybe when the stars align, when his team has a game a week and a fully fit squad he could achieve something better than the field but it is no more sensible to project out Carrick's future off the spring hot streak than it is to discount his coaching ability because he has struggled to cope with the first confluence of injuries, unfortunate results and player ill-discipline of his tenure.

Old Trafford seemed to have the right sense of it on Sunday. "It's Carrick you know," reverberated around the ground until the minute he was down the tunnel. Then it was both barrels for everyone else.

No one associated with Manchester United should apologize for having exacting standards. A well-run version of this club would make every decision based on improving their title-winning prospects either in the short or medium term. There should be no need to take the long way to the Premier League summit.

Having said all that, goodness it does not take much to send this club into a doom spiral of nostalgia and despair. When Lisandro Martinez served notice on Jason Wilcox and the hierarchy United had performed pretty well in defeat away to Atletico Madrid, a result that few in the Champions League field could credibly bemoan. Their form had wobbled but only a dodgy Erling Haaland goal had taken Manchester City past them and the last two Premier League results had been disappointing but not disastrous draws.

In short things were not going well but the difficulties were explicable. Up to the loss at the Metropolitano at least one of United's major problems was they had scored fewer goals than their expected goals (xG) for and conceded more than the xG value of their opponents shots. Their actual goal difference was minus-one, their expected goal difference was a shade under plus four. There's some heavy lifting being done in there by thrashing Ipswich Town and Sabah but the aggregate of a good team probably does contain a couple of thrashings as well as games where you play even against seemingly inferior teams like Fulham.

In short, just as United weren't as good as last season's rise to third place -- the defense started wobbling quite dramatically into the spring -- they aren't really as bad as 16th in the table, a point clear of the relegation zone might have you believe. A clear-eyed assessment both of the relative talent of United and the rest of the league would say that this is a good team vulnerable to a wobble. Just stay the course, keep calm in the dressing room and block out the noise.

But, of course... this is Manchester United we're talking about.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe certainly talked a good game when he finally got his hands on the sporting infrastructure at Old Trafford in February 2024, his $1.6 billion investment for around a quarter of the club affording him INEOS Group control of football operations at United. No longer would this be a club in hock to the first team head coach, the Ferguson way of thinking to be replaced by a brain trust that included the sporting director, "probably the recruitment guys" and, for reasons, the chief executive and Ratcliffe himself. "In modern football, you need to decide what's your path and stick to your path," the new minority owner insisted.

In the two and a half years since Manchester United's path has led them to: openly canvass the market for a replacement for manager Erik ten Hag, trigger an extension clause in his contract when they couldn't find anyone better, spend over $400 million outfitting the Dutchman with new players, sack him within four months, hire a coach in Ruben Amorim who had talked himself out of better jobs thanks to his insistence on playing a 3-4-3, finish 15th, sack Amorim just as their analytical profile was on an upswing because he had fallen out with his employers, bring in Carrick temporarily and then permanently, spend almost all their budget on midfielders, get dragged in public by Martinez.

That's just the condensed lowlights. It's fair to say that you don't hear much any more about Project 150, the ambitious vision to mark a century and a half of the club with a 21st top flight title. Perhaps by 2028 sporting director Wilcox will have got round to fixing the defense having blown so much of the 2025 summer budget on attack before then spending nearly $200 million on a midfield that needed upgrades but got Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba while the left back spot was left untouched.

It would say everything about the cataclysmic mismanagement at a senior level if Wilcox -- like so many at the club a man with little top level experience of the role he has been thrust into -- gets the man said to be his preferred choice to succeed Carrick, Eddie Howe.

The same Eddie Howe who spent a hugely successful two years with Dan Ashworth at Newcastle United. The same Dan Ashworth who Manchester United spent £4.1 million on the poaching of and, five months later, firing of. The same Manchester United who in INEOS' period running the show rank ninth in the Premier League for points, 10th for expected goal difference. Still, at least they sacked staff and cut costs. Who ever could have imagined that as a fix for a business' problems?

Speaking after Sunday's 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, Harry Maguire pulled no punches. "At the moment it's nowhere near good enough and something needs to change," he said. He's not wrong. And yet the only constants at this club sit second and first in our rankings. Cast your mind back to the 4-0 thrashing at the hands of Brentford in August 2022, Erik ten Hag's second game in charge and oh, what, half a dozen crises ago. The starting back four for Manchester United on that Saturday evening in west London? Diego Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw. The starting back four in draws against Fulham and Everton more than four years later? Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw.

There are players at this club who have seen off half a dozen permanent managers. Some might not have lasted that long but in their time they have been frozen out or put up for sale. Few have paid the price for inconsistency. Why would you respect the authority of the head coach if you have spent three or four years in the Old Trafford dressing room and seen so many cycle through without any apparent accountability for the playing staff. It seems notable that Cristiano Ronaldo's bombing out by Ten Hag was followed by one of the most impressive runs of results in the last half decade. Players discovered their actions had consequences and started playing like that.

Now, they talk like they are bulletproof. Imagine Martin Odegaard used a post-match interview to mouth off about Mikel Arteta's tactics. Would he ever play for Arsenal again? That's a question Mesut Ozil and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang can answer. When a player did not perform for Pep Guardiola's Manchester City, he was swiftly sold. Meanwhile United's squad is preserved in aspic. Their defense moves like it is.

These are not players who lack for talent. United's first choice attack rivals any bar Manchester City and Liverpool. Their midfield needs careful construction to mitigate for its lack of pace but it has quality. When the mood takes them Maguire, Martinez and Shaw are perfectly solid defenders. As the graphic above suggests, this is a team that can have moments of extreme competence. That is how United got to third a few months ago. Were they helped by the coach's tactics or the hierarchy's recruitment? Not really but that does not make these expensive, well-remunerated players innocent bystanders, unable to arrest the decline.

More than two decades after Malcolm Glazer loaded debt onto Manchester United to fund his purchase of the club, what has been accomplished beyond a steady degradation of this behemoth of English culture. Being owned by the Glazers, who have not put any money into the club since the takeover, is estimated to have cost the club at least $1.5 billion, much of it spent on servicing debt from the initial takeover. It should be noted that 15 major trophies have been won in the time the Glazers have owned the club but 10 of them came in the period where Ferguson's sheer magnetism held the club together.

There is an argument to be made that United's commercial income skyrocketed under current ownership and certainly this was a club that was among the first to realize that every region could have its own bespoke set of sponsors, that there was always another billboard or patch on the jersey to splash with a logo. Those brands were not, however, flocking to United because of anything the Glazers had done. United were the dominant force in English football at just the right moment to benefit from the Premier League moving from national to global obsession.

Far from custodians, the Glazers are the most deleterious of landlords. An extractive force, they provide minimal service and value while taking their management fees, dividends, repayments and then the riches Ratcliffe paid for a slice of the pie. All of their money could have gone into retaining United's preeminence in the English game or at least staving off the impact of their indifference. As if to make the metaphor particularly on the nose, on their watch Old Trafford has decayed such that the cost of renovation, an estimated $1.6 billion, might just make a case for the planned new stadium that no supporter seems to want.

A club that even in fallow years ranks among the top 10 revenue generators in football has found itself on a cost-cutting drive for which Ratcliffe is the face both because the Glazers' debt acts as a competitive drag and because ownership showed no interest nor aptitude in improving the on-field product. If the players represent a culture that is accountability-lite then it is ownership that enables it. When we start this piece by warning that nothing will change post-Carrick it is because we have seen enough to know that nothing changes until those who tolerate this degradation of Manchester United are no longer in a position of power.

#1273. NWSL Team of the Week: Croix Bethune breaks single-season assists record; Denver duo shines

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

No more second chances in the 2026 NWSL regular season. Decision Day is upon us, and before the chaos kicks off, players across the league are setting pitches ablaze with crucial performances. That means it's time to give out Attacking Third Team of the Week honors.

After weekly matches across the 2026 NWSL season, Attacking Third analysts will select players, a head coach, and an honorary captain based on weekend performances. Here you can find a mix of stats and data, analysis from our pundits, and highlights you may have missed over the weekend. If you're keeping track of who earned past honors, check out our previous team of the week.

It's been a wild year, and it feels like it's just getting started now that the postseason is rapidly approaching. That also means our team of the week honors will look slightly different following games moving forward. We'll hand out one more set of honors after Decision Day on November 1, but afterward, we'll be locked into playoffs and performances from the quarterfinals onward.

When it comes to the NWSL Shield, Gotham FC is taking the long road. If they manage to lift it, it'll be because they have a great goalkeeper to keep away any spoilers. Ann-Katrin Berger is back on the team of the week honors for keeping a newly eliminated and motivated Orlando Pride from deterring Gotham's quest for the title. She faced 19 shots, eight attempts on target, and made seven saves in a narrow but crucial victory.

Angel City's Evelyn Shores has become a bona fide two-way player this season and stands out on a backline that has Sarah Gorden and Savy King. She's back on the team of the week for another stellar performance, where she was instrumental in building up play and keeping the backline in shape. She led defenders on the team in duels (seven) and co-led in clearances (two) and interceptions (two).

Not that Tierna Davidson needed any more bullet points on her long resume for NWSL defender of the year, but scoring headers in the box was already on there. She did it again for Gotham FC and scored a decisive game-winner to keep the club ahead in the NWSL Shield race

Captain fantastic for @GothamFC second goal! 🎯Tierna Davidson doesn't miss in the box 💪Catch all the action on @CBSSportsNet 📺 pic.twitter.com/IJjecaVBDs

If you've ever heard of the iron woman concept in NWSL, then you're already familiar with Kaleigh Kurtz, but you might not be familiar with her dance moves. She showed them off after scoring her first goal with Denver Summit.

OUR IRON WOMAN GETS GER FIRST GOAL IN GREEN 🥲💚 pic.twitter.com/O1TTVwZMUV

Back on the team of the week is Janine Sonis after a two-assist performance for Denver Summit in a must-win game. Denver's playoff destiny is tricky, but possible, and Sonis is making sure she's leaving with something, her seventh and eighth assists of the year.

TASH FLINT, THAT'S YOURS. 💥 pic.twitter.com/J8fsKMFqz3

When the going gets tough this season, the tough runs away in fear of Jessie Fleming. The defensive midfielder has stepped up the club in a massive way between roster injuries and a red card suspension for Sophia Wilson. The Canadian international co-led the team in touches (66), led the team in recoveries (eight), and was a frequent outlet in building up play in a massive win over North Carolina.

Boston Legacy midfielder Alba Caño helped keep the team's spoiler reputation alive with an equalizer against San Diego. No NWSL Shield claimed on Boston's watch.

CAÑO HITS THE TOP CORNER 😤 pic.twitter.com/X3Ghk2G002

Seems like three points are easy to nab when Natasha Flint scores a break. The three points and goal differential could prove big in the playoff push.

Flexing her versatility over the weekend was Gisele Thompson for Angel City. Took her time on the ball and nailed the clinical finish.

Portland Thorns are a club with a lot of history, and Marie Muller etched her name into the chapter of big moments. A lethal blast on goal clinched a playoff spot for the team.

The head-coaching rumor mill has gone pretty silent after Angel City's impressive second-half run under interim manager Leif Smerud. The performance is going to make it difficult for the front office to move on from the interim magician.

#1272. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Florian Wirtz has scored or assisted in three consecutive games for the first time in his Liverpool career: 🅰️ vs LASK 🅰️ vs Brentford ⚽️ vs Villarreal https://t.co/woLWk2SGGL

It was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

It’s up there with one of the best I’ve played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot.

Whenever I get the ball and there’s an opportunity to go one v one or two v one, I believe in myself. I’ll just keep going and be ruthless.

Rio Ngumoha talking to Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime: “Definitely one of the best games I played. I enjoyed it.  Whenever I get the ball and go one v one, the more it makes the opposition worried.”

When he was reminded that he was the youngest Englishman to provide an assist in the Champions League, he said: “Records are amazing to break.”

And on playing on the right instead of the left wing: “It’s helped me a lot in training. Slowly I’m getting better on the right.”

And to hear the crowd chanting his name: “This stadium, we have the best fans. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.”

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

On the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Just the three minutes of added time to play, and Liverpool are probably grateful for that.

Could Liverpool be in for a nervous finish? Their defence is caught square again after a run in behind from Ayoze Perez, and Oluwaseyi was totally unmarked at the back post to apply a simple finish at silence Anfield.

Cody Gakpo threatens to score Liverpool’s fifth with an overhead free-kick, teed up by McConnell’s chipped cross to the back post, but he could not keep the attempt down.

The game is meandering towards its conclusion now, though a Villarreal goal would make things interesting.

Another Liverpool youngster enjoys a taste of first-team actions: James McConnell is on for Nyoni.
