Perez hits the post for Villarreal with only Alisson to beat, but the flag is raised for offside. I think that would have stood had he found the net, Van Dijk may have been playing him just onside.

Ngumoha receives his standing ovation, lovely moment for him. He has strong claims to be in Liverpool’s best XI. Bradley Barcola replaces him, not the player Villarreal’s tired defenders needed to see.

That is surely game over now, Liverpool heading for three Champions League wins from three. Former Newcastle United forward Ayoze Perez is now on for Villarreal. Ngumoha will be replaced by Barcola shortly and I’m sure he will receive a standing ovation.

The game has been transformed, and Villarreal are falling to pieces. They were guilty of losing possession far too cheaply, but Wirtz deserves credit for finishing with an authority he has been accused of lacking. Well struck across the goalkeeper with his left foot, his first Liverpool goal since April.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Ngumoha has been Liverpool’s best player on the night, although Cardona sold himself all too easily near the touchline. Ngumoha makes the right decision to pick out Mac Allister with a low cross, and the midfielder converts with the simplest of finishes.

Isak then replaces Koumas immediately after the goal.

Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal but Anfield also singing about Rio Ngumoha. He went past two Villarreal defenders to create that one. He has been outstanding.

There will be time to talk more about Rio Ngumoha – this is his best performance in a Liverpool shirt, a coming-of-age night if you will – but it cannot be overlooked how Alexis Mac Allister has been transformed. He was unrecognisable last season but now he is every inch the man who was a major cog in the push for the title.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Tsimikas with a dangerous, driven cross from the left which is just beyond the reach of Koumas. Liverpool knocking on the door.

Nyoni’s standing foot was slipping, but he made a clean connection on his shot from range and it whistled just wide of the foot of the post. Ngumoha then has the crowd cooing again, with another drop of the shoulder to beat his man.

Gravenberch found himself sweeping up as Liverpool’s last man, there. The second half has had a more conventional feel, Liverpool making the running as they shoot towards the Kop and their opponents soaking up the pressure. A game of fewer chances since the break.

Always helps having knowledge in close vicinity: a quick discussion with Rafa Benitez about Liverpool’s set up for the second period. Ryan Gravenberch hasn’t been moved to play as a right-back, even though you might think that is the case. Liverpool, essentially, are playing man-against-man. It is going to ask players to be brave on the ball and composed when they are in possession, as the slightest slip will lead to problems. It is high risk and high reward.

Not enough power in Gakpo’s strike from the edge of the area and Gulasci saves. Ngumoha looking such a threat again, attracting the attention of three or four yellow shirts and winning Liverpool another corner. Former Spurs player Juan Foyth has just been introduced by Villarreal.

Liverpool more industrious when they lose possession early in the half. Nyoni then produces a silky turn away from pressure deep in his own half which elicits an “ooohh” from the home fans.

Gravenberch took the ball off Ngumoha’s toes in the box, and the Dutchman’s shot from a tight angle was saved by Gulasci at his near post. I think Ngumoha deserved to have the shot himself after more great skill to find a yard.

Wirtz replaces Araujo, which could mean Gravenberch at right-back.

Oluwaseyi, another of Villarreal’s Canadian cohort, is on too. He replaces Saliba.

Florian Wirtz has been readied for action and will soon enter the fray. You would think these will be the kind of conditions in which he will excel. He needs to. Liverpool are lucky to be level.

03:54 - Georges Mikautadze's opener for Villarreal (03:54) is the second-earliest goal Liverpool have conceded at home in major European competition behind only Elpídio Silva's strike in the 3rd minute for Boavista in the UEFA Champions League in September 2001. Cold. https://t.co/NvKmS5jLap

Dreadful first 30 minutes from Liverpool but they have woken up since, and now they are strong favourites to win the game from here. Iraola’s selection gamble backfired somewhat, but he may well get away with it.

From the second phase of a corner, Ngumoha did well to keep the ball alive and lift a cross to the back post. Cardona tried to usher the ball behind and made the fatal mistake of letting it bounce in his penalty area, and Araujo sneaked in to score from close range.

The goalscorer Cardona makes a mistake to let Ngumoha’s cross drift to the backpost. That’s Liverpool’s equaliser from Ronald Araujo. As soon as Liverpool have got their act together they have looked dangerous.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

The crowd were impatient with him early in the half, but Gakpo is looking more of a threat now, Cruyff-turning away and shooting in the box but Veiga was across to block. Just the one minute of added time to play.

Gakpo wins Liverpool a free-kick in a shooting position left of centre, tripped after Nyoni had carried the ball well through midfield. Too much air on the attempt from Mac Allister, who a couple of minutes earlier fired not too far wide from 25 yards.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Really slick interplay from Villarreal again, and Moleiro’s shot from 25 yards is pushed over the bar by Alisson. You can pick holes in Liverpool, but Villarreal’s play deserves plaudits too.

Alexis Mac Allister grabs a goal back for Liverpool 🔴 Game 🔛 https://t.co/Ml9OYgbNq6

Liverpool have scarcely merited a goal but they have one via a set-piece. Alexis Mac Allister was up early at the near post and he produced a well-directed glancing header into the far corner. That changes the complexion of the game.

Great finish from Mac Allister. The opportunity for Gakpo to cross from the left - that won the corner - was made by Koumas’ hold-up play. First time he has really got hold of it and pinned the defender.

Another run from deep causes Liverpool’s defence problems, but Mikautadze took a touch when a first-time pass could have released the runner through on goal. More groans from the crowd when Tsimikas is caught on the ball.

Then Gakpo flashes a better ball across the face of goal, and Veiga glances it behind for a Liverpool corner.

Villarreal want a corner, and they should have one after a shot deflects off Araujo’s back. Goal kick given though.

Gakpo and Koumas are on the wrong wavelength, and there are groans from the crowd at another misplaced pass.

Liverpool need to dig themselves out of a hole now, Villarreal have cut them apart to score a simple second. Cardona, the left-back, with a run from deep, and Tsimikas was playing him onside. Cardona had all the time in the world to steady himself and roll the ball beyond Alisson.

Defensive calamity for Liverpool. Both Mikautadze and Cardona could have taken that through ball from Saliba and finished.

Straight through the heart of the defence 👀 Sergi Cardona doubles Villarreal's lead at Anfield 🤯 https://t.co/ZPHAkiLjN0

Liverpool far too easy to play through at the moment, Villarreal might not be an elite team but they have enough technique to pass and move well if given the time. Mikautadze lacks some pace up front, but has shown some silky touches. As Alan Shearer puts in on Amazon Prime: “Feels like a training match for Liverpool. So lazy. Where’s the urgency?”

Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. Aside from a couple of flurries following a Ronald Araujo tackle and a Rio Ngumoha dribble, it has been deathly quiet. Rafael Benitez, an architect of some of the wildest evenings here, is in the press box alongside Robbie Fowler and they are a reminder of how it used to be. Liverpool need to raise themselves to bring the crowd to life.

Ngumoha is the one ray of light for Liverpool so far, he has the beating of Villarreal left-back Cardona whenever he drops a shoulder. Gulasci palms his deflected cross over and Villarreal survive the corner.

The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Most of Liverpool’s attacks are being funnelled down their right so far, perhaps no surprise given that is where Ngumoha is stationed. Liverpool yet to test the goalkeeper, though.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

No need for Liverpool to panic just yet, plenty of time to turn this around, and Rio Ngumoha is going the right way about it. Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

Social media will be abuzz with scrutiny about Van Dijk now, as is always the case when he errs, but it won’t be taken into consideration that he has been one of Liverpool’s best players in these opening 10 games. What price would you make him to atone with a header at the other end later in the game?

Van Dijk has made two dreadful mistakes in the first four minutes and this time he is punished. Liverpool’s captain was trying to guide a header back to Alisson, but the ball shanked off his forehead at the wrong angle and dropped for Mikautadze in the box. The striker was free, and he finished well across Alisson. That was not in the script.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

Ryan Gravenberch has started the game in a more advanced midfield role with Nyoni and Mac Allister behind him. The home team are yet to string together a serious sequence of passes in the Villarreal half.

Liverpool trying to harry their opponents early on, but Van Dijk makes a hash of dealing with a simple long ball forward. Villarreal’s striker Mikautadze took too long to bring the ball down and the chance was gone with Jacquet closing him out.

It’s another young Liverpool team fielded in the Champions League, but they should have enough about them to see off this Villarreal side.

Out to get warm! ♨️ https://t.co/75qTJA6L42

Villarreal XI: Gulacsi, Mourino, Navarro, Veiga, Cardona, Saliba, Gueye, Buchanan, Comesana, Moleiro, Mikautadze

Subs: Junior, Costa, Freeman, Diatta, Gerard, Foyth, Akhomach, Macia, Oluwaseyi, Perez, El Jmili, Gaitan Diaz

Liverpool XI: Alisson; Araujo, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Gravenberch, Nyoni, Mac Allister; Ngumoha, Koumas, Gakpo

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Kerkez, Wirtz, Isak, Barcola, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Laffey

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

Roma once again threw away a two-goal Champions League advantage in a 3-2 defeat to Manchester United, as after dominating the first half, they repeated past mistakes.

Rodrigo Mora, Devyne Rensch and Leonardo Balerdi showed this was an attack-minded approach.

Manchester United were in crisis, without a win since September 10 and losing three on the bounce, including a 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como. Lenny Yoro returned from suspension, but Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu, Marcus Rashford, Manuel Ugarte and Luke Shaw were still out of action.

The deadlock was broken early when Roma’s trademark high press forced an error in midfield, then Rodrigo Mora floated a smart ball over the top to send unmarked Soulé clear to sweep past Sam Lammens at the near post.

#1270. Barcelona headline Women's Champions League Matchday 3 as league phase hits midway point

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League will reach the midway point of the league phase as Matchday 3 action kicks off Wednesday. The league phase table hardly looks like a final verdict, with only one team on maximum points, while some clubs are comfortable with split results and others are desperate to keep their campaigns alive. Matchday 3 offers an opportunity to either shake up the table or for clubs to separate themselves, with just four rounds of play left before February's knockout playoffs. Fans can watch all the action across CBS Sports platforms. Paramount+ will livestream matches all season, while select fixtures will also air on CBS Sports Golazo Network and CBS Sports Network. With Matchday 3 split across Wednesday and Thursday, here are four things we're keeping an eye on:

The reigning title holders return to the Champions League with even more hardware than before. The club and several players racked up plenty of honors at the Ballon d'Or ceremony on Monday. The club took home best club, manager Pere Romeu nabbed women's coach of the year, Vicky Lopez won best young talent and Cata Coll was named best goalkeeper.

Alexia Putellas, now with London City Lionesses, was awarded the women's Ballon d'Or, largely for her accomplishments during her final season with FC Barcelona, since the voting period ran from August 2025 to July 2026.

After defeating Paris FC 5-2 on Matchday 1, Barcelona followed up with a 6-0 blowout of Roma on Matchday 2. They're cruising during the league phase, especially with an attack powered by several standouts, including Lopez, Claudia Pina, Kerolin and Ewa Pajor.

Pajor, the Polish international, is now the all-time leading scorer in the Champions League's group and league phases, with 18 goals.

A new UWCL record for Ewa Pajor 👏Her 18th goal makes her the highest scorer in UWCL group/league phase history 👑Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/2LaFr3y5cj

They'll visit HB Koge on Thursday, and the Danish side is steadily growing into the competition after picking up its first win by beating Servette 5-1. The league phase leaders will be favorites to win, but Koge might not make it comfortable, as they play with nothing-to-lose energy.

OL Lyonnes made one of the biggest statements of the league phase so far with an opening-day 8-0 demolition of Servette, in which Melchie Dumornay scored a brace and Marie-Antoinette Katoto scored a hat trick. They're a Champions League mainstay and perennial contenders, but they were shut out by Chelsea on Matchday 2, with Blues goalkeeper Hannah Hampton putting her stamp on the tournament.

HANNAH HAMPTON STANDING ON HER HEAD 🤯Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/gd2mxcGJIF

OL Lyonnes will now face another club unbeaten in the league phase, Inter, on Wednesday. Inter have a win and a draw and have shown they are a plucky side to deal with, but if OL want to be lethal contenders, they have to make a statement against the tournament debutants. Dumornay's creativity and Katoto's clinical finishing, with U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes anchoring the midfield and a stacked roster around them, will be a tough challenge for any team, especially those newer to the league phase. Chelsea, meanwhile, have to contend with Roma, an Italian squad that's well on its way to another Champions League crashout, showing little improvement in year two of the new league phase format with just one draw over two games. If the Blues could keep OL off the scoreboard, they should be confident they can do the same against Roma, and if they don't, it'll bring more questions about the club's ability to manage Champions League expectations. German side Bayern Munich welcome Real Madrid in a showdown that could tip the league phase table. Bayern had a chance to make an opening-day statement but instead gave up a two-goal lead and settled for a draw against Manchester City, before picking up a crucial win away against Benfica in Portugal. Matches in this competition have often been won or lost late, and veteran Pernille Harder had her say for Bayern at Benfica, scoring her 50th UWCL goal in the 3-0 victory.

50 UWCL GOALS FOR PERNILLE HARDER 🌟She becomes just the fourth player in competition history to reach the milestone 👏Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/wG9RWk22sl

Real Madrid's two consecutive draws in the competition leave everyone wanting more. Colombia international Linda Caicedo is elite and has consistently shown her quality over the two matches, and if she and Felicia Schroder continue to build chemistry in attack, they'll be a dangerous combo to deal with.

The meeting between the German and Spanish clubs on Wednesday will be a key fixture to watch, as a win for either could put it in a more favorable position in the league phase table at the halfway point.

There were plenty of doubts around Paris Saint-Germain heading into the tournament, given their steep fall from Champions League grace. After a miserable campaign last season, the Parisians got off to another worrisome start with a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, in which they trailed for over 70 minutes before equalizing from the penalty spot. They quickly followed that up with a five-goal win over OH Leuven on Matchday 2, and now find themselves in a far better position than they were last year. Next up is Manchester City, a side that is still on the hunt for its first win of the tournament. Two sides carefully rebuilding their UWCL pedigree could produce either a cagey matchup or a momentum-shifting performance. Arsenal continue to baffle on the pitch. After a smash-and-grab for all three points on opening day against underdogs HB Koge, the Gunners were challenged by Paris FC in a 2-2 draw the following matchday. Winning ugly doesn't hide the fact that this is a team that has struggled to break opponents down, despite a talented roster, and it raises fair questions about manager Renee Slegers and her tactical approach. Goals from Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway help, but there is more that's expected from the group that won the UWCL title in 2025, even with Mariona Caldentey managing an injury at the moment. If they struggle against Benfica on Wednesday, it'll cast more doubt on the club's direction this season.

The bottom of the league phase table is already somewhat crowded, even with some unexpected clubs at the moment, but that's what makes the midway point of the tournament so exciting. Manchester City and Real Madrid might steal eyeballs, as neither team can keep drawing for much longer, but former dark horse BK Hacken and last year's dancing debutants OH Leuven have struggled to find the net. Hacken join Servette with zero points through two matchdays and will face Paris FC on Thursday. Paris FC are eager to take the next step in the UWCL, from unpredictable underdogs to bona fide contenders. Whoever drops points in the head-to-head could be out of the race for the top 12 in the league phase.

#1269. Martin O'Neill's greatest mistake was staying after winning the league

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:24 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 14:51 EDT, 3 November 2026

Winning the league title in such dramatic fashion on the final day of last season, Martin O’Neill should have recognised the moment for what it was. The End.

In a chaotic season where he had rescued Celtic from oblivion not once but twice, that was the moment when the credits should have rolled.

The blockbuster Hollywood finale. The perfect opportunity to go out in a blaze of glory and sail off into the sunset, his legacy not only secure but further enhanced.

His decision to stay on as manager this season has proven to be a mistake. In his heart of hearts, O’Neill must realise this. The whole thing is done. Finished. Finito. Terminado, as one of his predecessors would have said.

On the back of the 2-0 defeat to Falkirk last weekend, it has now reached the point where O’Neill’s continued presence at the club is damaging his legacy.

The fans are turning on him. They don’t care what he did for the club 20-odd years ago. They aren’t interested in his wisecracks. They don’t want to hear nostalgic tales of old about how things used to be.

They care only about the here and now and about what they are watching on the pitch. Now mired in a run of three wins in their last ten matches, O’Neill’s side are, if anything, actually getting worse.

O’Neill’s argument about still being top of the league is one of deflection, denial and delusion. Complete and utter claptrap. It is an insult to the intelligence of Celtic supporters.

Martin O'Neill's Celtic team lead the table but have struggled to convince

This is the problem. If there is solid evidence to support the claims that he has lost the faith of the players, then he is also rapidly losing the faith of the fans.

In a way, it is sad that it should come to this. The man is 74 years old. He didn’t ask to be thrust back into the spotlight. At least, not initially.

On two occasions, he answered an SOS call from Dermot Desmond last season. He came back and he did exactly what was asked of him.

If Celtic had any sort of competent succession plan in place, there wouldn’t even have been a conversation around O’Neill’s future towards the end of last season.

It would have been a case of shaking his hand, thanking him enormously for a heroic contribution, before being serenaded by supporters one last time after winning a league and cup double.

Yet, going back to those final few weeks of last season, it was clear O’Neill had the bug for it once again. He was never going to walk away, and nor were the board ever going to turn him down.

In the end, the situation needed one of two things to happen. It either needed O’Neill to save himself from his own desires, and have some sense and foresight about how the club was being run, or it needed Celtic to show some vision and make a proper long-term appointment.

In the absence of both, it was the blind leading the blind. O’Neill hung around primarily to have another crack at Europe, the Celtic board thought they had a bulletproof shield by retaining the services of a club icon.

The argument that kept on being trotted out at the time centred on how winning the league title meant that O’Neill had earned the right to stay on.

But that fundamentally missed the point. Of course he had earned the right. He’s Martin O’Neill. Only Jock Stein stands above him in the pantheon of the club’s all-time greatest managers.

Fans adored him (yes, past tense). But just because he had earned the right doesn’t mean it was the right thing to do. That’s the key difference.

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill lifts the league trophy back in May

Whenever Manchester United inevitably sack Michael Carrick, let’s suppose for a second that Sir Alex Ferguson comes in and takes charge for a few games.

Everything goes well, the team start winning games again, everyone starts getting those old feelings coming back.

But would it mean that the right thing to do is to hand Sir Alex the job for another season? Of course it wouldn’t.

The failure to separate that nostalgia and love for O’Neill from what was required moving into this season was a catastrophic error of judgment on Celtic’s part.

The club had absolutely no idea how to move forward in the summer – just like they would have absolutely no idea who to appoint now if O’Neill was to be relieved of his duties.

In the past, Celtic sacked Tommy Burns. They sacked Billy McNeill. The belief that O’Neill could not suffer a similar fate is hugely naive.

Right now, a growing section of the fanbase view him as little more than an extension of Desmond. His status as a club icon is fading.

Over the weekend, a couple of articles surfaced from a few years ago when O’Neill was sacked as Nottingham Forest manager in 2019.

They spoke of how O’Neill eventually lost the dressing room and of how the players were left bemused by his lack of detail on the tactical side of the game.

Some Celtic fans view O'Neill as little more than an extension of major shareholder Dermot Desmond

The parallels with this current Celtic side are obvious. Just look at the comments from Callum McGregor and Cameron Carter-Vickers over recent weeks.

They are a team with absolutely no tactical identity – and it’s difficult to see how this gets any better for as long as O’Neill, along with coaches Shaun Maloney and Mark Fotheringham, remain at the helm.

O’Neill attended a Q&A session at a supporter’s club in Greenock on Monday night, along with chief executive Michael Nicholson and chairman Brian Wilson.

A bizarre announcement from Celtic yesterday claimed that the questioning had been ‘hard but fair’ as supporters voiced their concerns about the current malaise.

The one man who continues to dodge the Paxman treatment is, of course, Desmond himself, the club’s largest shareholder who operates as the commander-in-chief.

And the one question which is now becoming painfully unavoidable is this: what grounds are there for Martin O’Neill to continue as Celtic manager?

#1267. UCL | Feyenoord 0-3 Inter: Strong Nerazzurri statement

Inter made a strong Champions League statement with a 3-0 victory away to Feyenoord thanks to Yann Bisseck, Pio Esposito and Piotr Zielinski goals.

The Nerazzurri mood was grim after losing the Derby della Madonnina to rivals Milan 3-1 on Saturday, having lost their first two Champions League games, with a scraped 1-0 victory over Shakhtar Donetsk. Alessandro Bastoni saw red in that game and was therefore suspended, with Lautaro Martinez, Curtis Jones, Luis Henrique and John Stones still injured.

Feyenoord had already beaten Como here 3-2 this season, but Jakub Moder, Bart Nieuwkoop, Gijs Smal, Jeremiah St. Juste, Thomas Beelen and Jordan Bos were unavailable.

It was the perfect start for Inter, because they took the lead within eight minutes. Yann Bisseck pressed high to win it back, turned between two and swept the finish into the far bottom corner with the inside of the left foot. It was the defender’s first ever Champions League goal.

The centre-back with a centre-forward finish 👌 Yann Bisseck gives Internazionale the lead after just 8 minutes🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6uvO9 https://t.co/p3PfQyWGsn

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) November 3, 2026

Federico Dimarco had a couple of shots charged down at the near post, but Anis Hadj Moussa dribbled past the Italian to force a tricky save out of Josep Martinez at the near post.

Inter doubled their lead when Djed Spence got down the right and stood up a deflected cross for the Francesco Pio Esposito header from four yards, despite Feyenoord complaints of his physical tussle with the defender to get on the end of it.

Piotr Zielinski drilled just wide, then tested the goalkeeper from distance with another trademark scorcher before half-time.

Spence stung the goalkeeper’s gloves at the near post after a strong run, but after several attempts came close, Zielinski finally got his goal with a ferocious strike from the edge of the area.

Pio Esposito had the ball in the net again on 66 minutes, but was offside when meeting the Dimarco roll across from a couple of yards.

#1266. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

There may be some truth in that, but Carrick’s response felt the most accurate assessment of the lot and will certainly chime with supporters who have long questioned how and why so many United sides, regardless of the manager, reach a point where running, intensity and urgency seem optional. “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” Carrick said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

Having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Nico Paz scores a stunner to get Como ahead against Manchester United within 2 minutes! 😱 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/ikH9MVg6cB

You looked at Como and it was clear every player knew their job and role and went about it with relish. There were patterns of play, they ran, there was intensity and movement and they were quicker to everything.

Paz scored the first and third goals and set up a wondrous second for Tasos Douvikas that showcased Como’s talent at the same time as underlining United’s myriad fault lines. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. Jacobo Ramón completed the rout before Joshua Zirkzee scored the most hollow of goals for United late on.

Como extend their lead to 2-0 against Manchester United early in the second half! Anastasios Douvikas gets the goal 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/2O9qRG75tG

United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

Nico Paz capitalises on a mistake from Carlos Baleba to extend Como's lead against Manchester United to 3-0 😱 He's been involved in each goal 👏 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/D7kD8PGtcY

For Como, who were playing in Italy’s third tier five years ago, this was one of the greatest nights in their history. For United, it was one of the worst. Carrick may pay a heavy price for it, but there are far greater problems than the manager at this football club.

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

#1265. Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe apologizes after Mao meme comments amid growing backlash in China

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe issued an apology Tuesday after comments he made about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong led several sponsors to drop him and drew a backlash from Chinese state television. The day after the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony, which saw Mbappe leave the London Palladium empty-handed, began with an international drama involving China, Mbappe and LaLiga. It all started when Mbappe told French talk show "The Bridge" that the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." The clip also showed Mbappe's face on an image resembling Mao. To put that into context, a recurring joke, repeated in multiple memes, associates Mbappe with the word "dictator" for his influence in the sport and for how he interacts with teammates and players. During the 2026 World Cup, 2025 Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele called him "Mbappe Mobut," referring to Mobutu, the dictator who ran the Democratic Republic of Congo for more than 30 years. In September, Mbappe addressed the memes in an interview with France Football, saying that while he understood the jokes, they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people. There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history. Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." Two Chinese brands that have deals with the French striker issued statements condemning the player's statements. Mengniu, the country's largest dairy producer, wrote that it, "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." Later on Tuesday, drinks giant Dongpeng issued a statement as well. "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." According to the state-owned Global Times newspaper, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV's apps won't feature news related to the player, and the broadcaster will also stop streaming LaLiga matches.

Mao is obviously one of the most famous figures in modern China's history. He founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led the Communist Party until his death in 1976. Much has changed in China since his death, but the Chinese Communist Party still governs the country and sees jokes and memes about Mao as an insult to the party and the nation. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said, "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

The French striker issued a statement about the matter: "During a recent interview with me, I commented on an image of myself, but my comment was not appropriate, and I now realise that it hurt the feelings of many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone whom my words upset, as that was never my intention at all. I hold deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I express my sincere regret."

LaLiga also issued a statement, defending the agreement they still have in place with Chinese state television. "LALIGA deeply regrets the offence caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé's recent comments. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. Within the scope of our institutional responsibility, we apologise on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs. Spanish football stands for respect, coexistence and unity among people from all cultures. We extend our respect to China, its institutions and its people, and deeply value the support of the millions of fans who follow us every week. We reaffirm our commitment to a relationship built over many years. We are working with our partners and institutional counterparts in China to address this situation. Furthermore, in collaboration with clubs and players, we will introduce an awareness and communication protocol aimed at promoting respect for different cultures and helping to prevent similar situations in the future."

LaLiga president Javier Tebas, who recently also had multiple public disagreements with Real Madrid, wrote on X he "cannot allow the actions of an individual to tarnish this relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs competing in our professional leagues and the millions of Chinese fans. We are taking all measures within our power and working directly with our partners and counterparts in China to resolve this situation."

Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. #1264. Are Brighton a Premier League contender? Manchester City EFL Cup match will be biggest test yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Is this the year Brighton and Hove Albion make the leap? In their 10th season in the Premier League, the Seagulls have long since moved on from being a side well run enough to keep its distance from the relegation race. Now they might reasonably aspire to another step forward, away from the mass of sides just outside the premium European places and into real contention for Champions League qualification. Indeed, if you are a more exuberant Brighton fan, the question you might be asking yourself is not whether your side has made the leap but whether it has bounded up two tiers over the course of one summer. After all, they sit third in the Premier League table with the division's best attack and its third-best defense; combine those and you have a plus-16 goal difference. Their nearest rival by that metric, Manchester City, is at plus-11. Beat City in the second of this week's doubleheader with Enzo Maresca's side and they will be two points off the league leaders, though Arsenal might well open up a gap. Then again, what do Brighton have to fear from the champions? They've already smashed them 3-0 this season. Even their 2-0 defeat to Liverpool did little to quell Brighton's momentum. Not for the first time in his managerial career, Fabian Hurzeler couldn't resist a snipe at the manager of a big-six opponent in defeat, but he did have a point when he argued that "there was one team who really tried to create and try to win this game." The Seagulls went down swinging at Anfield, drawing seven shot blocks from Andoni Iraola's side. It really was not an exaggeration to say that if Yasin Ayari or Charalampos Kostoulas had scored early on, this might have been another famous win for the boys from the south coast.

Does this all sound too good to be true? Well, then it probably is. Admittedly, Hurzeler's side had looked primed to push on at the end of last season, an impressive run of results in March and April securing an eighth-placed finish and Conference League football. Then, in customary Brighton fashion, their best players left. Danny Welbeck had been their leading scorer, Jan Paul van Hecke the leader in league minutes and a crucial ball progressor, and while Carlos Baleba had endured a down year in which he had battled injuries, he still looked the most likely to ascend to a Moises Caicedo/Alexis Mac Allister level in Brighton's long line of breakout talent in midfield. Brighton could be trusted to replace the players they sold well. Swapping out Van Hecke for Luka Vuskovic already looks like the greatest of swindles on Tottenham, who are happy enough with what they have, even if they might have let the next great center back slip away. It is arguably easier, though, to deal with players you have lost for a fee than with those snared from you by injury. Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh were the star wingers in last season's side, the former top 10 in the league for expected possession value added, the latter top 10 for take-ons. These wingers were critical for getting the ball into the box and creating threat when they got there. Injuries mean they have yet to take the field this season. You should not be able to cope with the loss of this much talent for so long. Some of Hurzeler's fixes have been ingenious. Maxim De Cuyper carried plenty of attacking thrust from left back, and after dalliances with a more advanced role last season, he has been converted to it permanently. The careful, steady integration of Kostoulas and Diego Gomez has paid dividends too. Meanwhile, at 35, Pascal Gross is as effective as he has ever been, with four assists and three goals already in this season's Premier League. Gross' pressing has also been critical to Brighton's success. According to data provided to CBS Sports by Gradient, the German international has made eight pressures leading to dangerous situations, placing him in the 99th percentile among Premier League players this season. Kostoulas and De Cuyper are similarly willing runners off the ball, adding up to a team that is even more energetic without the ball this season than it was last. In 2025-26, Brighton led the Premier League in passes per defensive action with 9.3, according to Wyscout. This season they also lead the division in this pressing metric, allowing opponents an average of 7.6 passes per defensive action. It is for that reason that only Wednesday's opponents, Manchester City, allow the other team fewer active minutes in possession than Brighton's 21.5.

Brighton's pressing intensity also means it is not that much of a surprise that they lead the league in counterattacking goals. As they do in goals from corners. As they do in higher-value chances where the shot is worth 0.1 expected goals or higher. As they do too in shots from outside the box. It all looks great, but then the sample size is still only eight games. That might be enough to form the outline of a conclusion in normal circumstances, but Brighton are one of only two teams in the league to have had a man advantage in two games so far this season. It should be said that both Aston Villa and Coventry looked like beaten teams when their player saw red, but we have to take the data set with a pinch of salt when over 10% of it involves Brighton having one more player. (There was also an impressive 33 minutes with 10 men against Sunderland, in which they held on to and ultimately added to a 1-0 lead.) So we should take some of their headline numbers under advisement. Drill deeper and there might be more factors to consider. Brighton lead the league in scoring and are second in xG, but there is a big gap between their 16.2 xG and 23 goals. This is a year in which Brighton's goal-of-the-season contest might be a reasonable proxy for the Premier League's as a whole (Lewis Dunk leads the way for me, Clive). Their shooting form was typified by that 3-0 win over Arsenal. They at least matched the champions in the first half, but they led 2-0 because both Gross and Kostoulas walloped shots in from range. You're not building a title challenge on that. Nor are you necessarily doing the same when you look porous at the other end. It isn't just that Brighton have allowed 11.4 xG to their opponents and are riding a run of shot-stopping that seems unlikely to continue even for a goalkeeper of Bart Verbruggen's quality. Hurzeler's side are also allowing the third-highest xG per shot of any team in the division. Much of that is a function of a worrying set-piece defense, but they are not much better from open play either, allowing 0.117 xG per shot, 10% above the Premier League average. When a team breaks their press like Chelsea did early in the season, that's when they end up in trouble. You don't compete for titles when you are giving up what Brighton are giving up defensively, but then that is a ludicrous conceit in the first place. What is clearly no longer ludicrous is the idea that this team might regularly beat Man City in a one-off match, whether that be the rotated outfit Enzo Maresca is due to field in the EFL Cup on Wednesday or the full-strength outfit that will presumably welcome them back to the Etihad on Saturday afternoon. Indeed, in the reasonably likely event that a sanction obliterates City's standing in this season's Premier League, Brighton could comfortably find themselves among the four or five Champions League qualifiers. The likes of Bournemouth, Nottingham Forest and Brentford are at best performing around Brighton's level so far this season in xG terms but have not picked up anywhere near as many points. Maybe the quality of Liverpool shows down the stretch. Perhaps Xabi Alonso simplifies things at Chelsea. Even then, that probably leaves a fifth spot for an English team to advance to the top tier. There is no question now that Brighton look better placed than anyone else to claim it, propelling themselves into a new class of club. If the experience of the last 10 seasons is anything to go on, this club tends to establish itself quite firmly when it moves up in the world.

#1263. Gasperini: ‘Roma will learn more from Man Utd defeat than Real Madrid’

Gian Piero Gasperini insists Roma ‘will learn’ from their Champions League collapse at Manchester United, more so than when doing the same with Real Madrid. ‘Disappointment sets in.’

This is evidently now a pattern for the Giallorossi, not just in the Champions League with the 3-1 advantage fumbled against Real Madrid in seven minutes, but in Serie A too when caught for draws after going in front.

They were in control at Old Trafford, leading 2-0 after 18 minutes with Matias Soulé and the Donyell Malen penalty, with several opportunities to score a third.

However, once Bruno Fernandes converted a soft spot-kick, which was first saved by Devis Vasquez only to be retaken for encroachment, it was a different match, and Matheus Cunha’s late double secured the first Manchester United victory since September 10.

“It was a different game to Real Madrid, where it all happened in the last seven or eight minutes from corner kicks, and there were no real signs of the comeback,” Gasperini told Sky Sport Italia.

“This time, it was above all after the penalty that Manchester United had this sudden surge of enthusiasm, and we were unable to keep up with it.”

Considering it happened twice in the last three Champions League games, it cannot be a coincidence that Roma crumble when leading.

“I don’t think it’s a coincidence, but I also think they were different matches. This evening, we didn’t have the strength to press their strikers the way we did in the first half, plus the penalty and the error for the equaliser really turned the tide.

“There is always going to be 15-20 minutes against Manchester United when you’re under pressure, and if you can emerge unscathed from it, you’ll be fine.”

The defeat to Real Madrid was dominated for longer, yet because of the calibre of opponent, it feels as if this loss to Manchester United hurts more for Roma because it was such a wasted opportunity.

“Honestly, we learned more from this match than the one with Real Madrid. That felt unpredictable, whereas at times today when Old Trafford was pushing on the team, we need to be able to handle these situations better in future,” conceded Gasperini.

“They made modifications at half-time and had nothing left to lose, so they pressed high, so perhaps we should’ve made more of long balls in that situation. The problem was we were no longer able to stick to their reference points, so they had the better on pressing, not letting us play, but also on their attacks. That created some problems for us, we probably should’ve tried to interrupt their rhythm a bit more with some extra challenges and slow the tempo down.

“The momentum of the match changed with the penalty and the incident for 2-2.”

Another recurring mistake Roma are guilty of is crumbling the moment something goes wrong, as within 60 seconds of the Bruno Fernandes penalty, Bryan Mbeumo hit the woodwork, and three minutes after the equaliser was the winning goal.

“That’s true, it happened against Real Madrid too, so perhaps there is a bit of disappointment that sets in when you see the victory drifting away. Again, we need the team to take the pressure of a result at all costs off itself, so this game will help us learn more than others,” confirmed Gasperini.

It was not the best build-up to this match, seeing as both Mile Svilar and Pierluigi Gollini were ruled out by injury, so Vasquez had to make his club debut as third-choice shot-stopper.

Paulo Dybala, Manu Koné and Lorenzo Pellegrini were also out, and Devyne Rensch limped off with a muscular issue in the first half, but Nahuel Molina wasn’t introduced.

“Molina is an international, but Rensch started very well and had this injury, so I chose Lulli and that used up a slot. Wesley played well defensively, this was not the reason we struggled.”

#1261. Chivu: ‘Inter were the best version of ourselves’ in 3-0 victory at Feyenoord

Cristian Chivu feels Inter were ‘the best version of ourselves’ in tonight’s 3-0 Champions League victory away to Feyenoord, but ‘consistency is what brings results.’

The Nerazzurri were under pressure in Rotterdam and needed to send a response after their 3-1 defeat to Milan in the Derby della Madonnina on Saturday.

It was certainly that, as they dominated against a Feyenoord side that beat Como here 3-2 and has a notoriously strong home record.

Yann Bisseck, Francesco Pio Esposito and Piotr Zielinski were all on target in a pretty comfortable encounter, and Esposito had another goal ruled inches offside on a Federico Dimarco pass.

Notably, Inter have been criticised for their bad starts to games and it was not since August that they had scored in the opening eight minutes.

“We have certain values, we understood certain things and put them on the pitch,” Chivu told Sky Sport Italia.

“That doesn’t mean we haven’t done well so far this season. We tried to be the best version of ourselves, it worked today with organisation, intensity and everything we needed for a strong performance in a stadium that is not easy to play in.”

What did the coach mean when saying the team understood certain things?

“We always have discussions after every game, whether it goes well or badly, we try to correct errors and build on our strengths. Sometimes it goes better than others, perhaps we understood what wasn’t going as well,” said Chivu.

“The Inter world, the club owners, the fans, we are all aware of the values of these players who want to fly the flag high, that has never been in doubt.”

Another recurring problem so far this season has been a lack of consistency throughout the 90 minutes, but this evening they always seemed to be in control.

“Consistency is what brings results, it gives you self-confidence and belief in what you are doing, it is what we are looking for at this moment. This game gives us a big boost of confidence in what we are building, so we know football can take you down some strange paths, but you must be able to react and get back onto the right path,” concluded the Inter coach.

This result allows Inter to climb up the Champions League table, but they still have only six points from four games, so it will be a fight to the end in order to scrape into the next round.

A team like inter with all talents is struggling to win a match, beating Fayenoord looks like lifting UCL cup,wake up and do more compete with Europe’s best teams because you have all it takes

#1260. Celtic boss Martin O'Neill and board given 'hard but fair' grilling by fans in Greenock

Published: 15:16 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 15:36 EDT, 3 November 2026

Martin O’Neill and senior Celtic board members were subjected to ‘hard but fair’ questioning in a meeting at Greenock Celtic Supporters’ Club on Monday night, the club have revealed.

The manager was joined by chairman Brian Wilson, chief executive Michael Nicholson, chief financial officer Chris McKay and other club officials for a two-and-a-half-hour question-and-answer session that revolved around recruitment, transfer policy, communications and the club’s ambitions and strategy.

Representatives from Greenock, Port Glasgow, Gourock, Johnny Doyle, Port Glasgow Hibs and Largs supporters clubs were among around 120 Celtic fans who attended ‘to seek information and voice concerns’.

Martin O'Neill and the Celtic board met supporters in Greenock

The meeting came just a day after Celtic’s 2-0 defeat at Falkirk left them with just three wins from their past 10 matches in all competitions.

O’Neill, whose own position has come under intense scrutiny recently, told the Hoops’ website: ‘I asked to attend the meeting because I want to meet supporters as much as I possibly can.

‘We have had a few difficult weeks in recent times and I understand our supporters’ frustrations, but my resolve and the commitment of the players is as strong as ever to continue to bring success and progress to the club.’

Wilson vowed that the club would take on board concerns raised by supporters.

‘We were grateful to the Greenock Celtic Supporters’ Club for hosting this event in a way that allowed everyone to make their points, many of them critical, and to ask questions which we did our best to answer,’ the chairman said. ‘We didn’t expect an easy ride and didn’t get one, but the meeting was conducted in a constructive and mutually respectful way and the messages delivered by supporters will be taken on board and learned from.’

#1259. Defensive flaws threaten to derail Chelsea during Xabi Alonso's first season ahead of Liverpool showdown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As Chelsea and Liverpool meet in the EFL Cup, it's a good time to take a look at the beginning of the Xabi Alonso era at the club. On the surface, it has had its highs, like a 5-1 victory over Bournemouth, but it has also brought lows, such as losing to Tottenham while Cole Palmer picked up a red card. As the Blues look to return to Champions League play, it's becoming very apparent that they're missing Enzo Fernandez following his departure to Manchester City over the summer. There isn't much that could've been done to keep the Argentine, as he wanted to follow his former manager to the Etihad, but the fallout has been serious, as only teams in the relegation race are allowing more goals per 90 minutes than Chelsea's 1.71.

With a Liverpool side that's waking up under Andoni Iraola, as Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola find their footing while Alexander Isak gets back to his best, it's a challenge that could break a defense that has already been struggling and see the cup run come to an end for the Blues, especially since Emi Martínez will still be sidelined with a broken jaw after being added from Aston Villa to upgrade the defense.

Date: Wednesday, Oct. 28 | Time: 4 p.m. ETLocation: Anfield -- Liverpool, EnglandLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Liverpool +120; Draw +275; Chelsea +185

Cole Palmer will be suspended, while Joao Pedro and Reece James will also miss the match, straining Alonso's already thin squad. Missing just one of these players would give Alonso tough decisions to make, but the entire group puts an already weak defense at risk. At their best, Chelsea want to be on the front foot pressing, and their open-play defense has been able to get back and stay in position when needed, thanks to Maxence Lacroix being able to organize the backline. The Frenchman usually stays back when the attack goes forward and is able to fly into tackles to protect his keeper.

The issue has been set plays. When Martinez isn't in net, Chelsea's other keepers lack command of the box. It wouldn't be a huge problem if they weren't giving up set-piece opportunities with their constant fouling. Add it all up, and while there's been clear improvement under Alonso, Chelsea still have a long way to go to make it back to Europe's premier competition.

Monaco did scupper some of their plans by pulling out of a deal to sell Lamine Camara to the Blues when it seemed like Folarin Balogun was going to Everton. While Camara would've helped with these issues, Alonso also needs to set the team up to play more directly and lean into the strength of his front three. Ceding possession to go direct does expose defensive flaws, but that's also something the Blues need to do at this stage, since scoring goals is the best form of defense they have.

When there's time to add more to the squad and use some of this Fernandez cash, this could change, but until then, Chelsea are among the most unusual sides in the world, which will lead to a fascinating tie with Liverpool. It's one they need to win, and a loss would confirm what the numbers already show. The Blues can't keep getting away with it, because this isn't a Champions League team yet. All signs point to them getting there, but doing it this season would be ahead of schedule and down to struggles by teams like Manchester United. With Aston Villa turning things around in ninth, the table could look quite different a month from now.

#1258. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

#1257. Harry Kane is 'still processing' his Ballon d'Or win, so he went back to the only thing he knows

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MUNICH – Less than an hour into a casual second-round cup match, a pocket of Bayern Munich fans in one corner of the Allianz Arena had moved on from reveling over Michael Olise's brace against second-division side Magdeburg. Their attention was instead on the group of substitutes who were warming up behind the opponent's goal and one person in particular.

It was a likely place for Harry Kane to spend a Wednesday evening, no matter the circumstances. Considering Bayern's relative strengths, the coaching staff had already hoped to give Kane the night off, especially with Borussia Dortmund awaiting this weekend and a trip to Atletico Madrid in the UEFA Champions League coming up on Tuesday. This was no ordinary midweek cup game, though, the pre-match guard of honor from his teammates as clear a sign as any of the occasion. It was Kane's first time back since winning the Ballon d'Or on Monday, doing so in his hometown of London.

The warm-ups were the only glimpse the crowd got of him on Wednesday, Bayern getting business done swiftly with a 6-1 win. Yet, Kane's appearance on the sidelines alone was celebratory, both after becoming the first Englishman to win the individual accolade in 25 years and the first player from the Bundesliga to do it since Matthias Sammer accomplished the feat in 1996. It was the type of thing that required an afterparty that allegedly stretched long after a delayed, bloated ceremony came to an end at around 11 p.m. local time, though Kane insisted he "didn't party too hard." It also allowed him to follow up a crowning achievement the only way he knows how – "straight back to work."

Kane trained on Tuesday and would have been ready to play if called upon on Wednesday, and is expected to prepare as usual for Saturday's clash with Dortmund. It comes as little surprise for a player who has rarely chased individual accolades. He has repeatedly insisted that his goal every four years is to win the World Cup with England, not the golden boot and left boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur for greater collective opportunities with Bayern in 2023 despite being just 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League goalscoring record at the age of 30. The spotlight has followed Kane for much of his career but he has always chosen to share it. There is no flexibility with the attention the Ballon d'Or carries, though; only one person can win it, no matter how team-oriented that person happens to be.

"It's strange," Kane said. "It's not my normal thing to enjoy. Even the guys, when I was walking out to warm up and they're all there clapping. I don't know. I get quite, maybe, embarrassed by it, but I know this is a big deal and I felt that obviously in the event, I felt that since with the reception and how much messages I've got from not just friends and family but people sending my number to other coaches and people just that have known me or know of me and they all wanted to just say well done. I think I'm still processing everything, to be honest, but look, I know it's a really big deal so I appreciate everyone, and you know, even on Saturday, I know we're going to do something before the game and all this, and it's important to do because it's a big celebration as well."

Even in his hometown on Monday, surrounded both by loved ones and his Bayern teammates who chanted his name in the London Palladium as Ronaldo revealed he had won the sport's ultimate individual prize, Kane felt out of place.

"A lot of nerves and just different emotions compared to a football match or anything like that and a lot of waiting around and just trying to picture what it'd be like if I did win but honestly, just really special," he said. "The support I've had from friends, family, fans, text messages, social media has just been overwhelming almost."

There is a lot Kane has not considered about life post-Ballon d'Or, either, like where the trophy might rest or what will come of the gold-flaked schnitzel that was made by a Bavarian restaurant and delivered to his home.

"I didn't actually eat it yesterday," he said. "With the match being today, I have a routine of what I eat and stuff but now, obviously, I appreciate it. It's a nice tradition that we have so to have a gold one, let's just keep them coming."

True to form, Kane has found the most comfort in a busy week in a return to his familiar routine.

"I think just being back to football," he said. "It feels like the Freiburg game [on Sunday] was six weeks ago. So much has happened in 48 hours. It was nice just to be back. A bit of normality, seeing the fans, getting a reception before the game, obviously, and then honestly just being back with the boys and just watching football and watching the boys play again so it's been a whirlwind of a 48 hours, and it's nice to just kind of be here and feel at home again."

He admitted he needs to add a new item to the routine at home, though – protecting the Ballon d'Or from his four children, aged nine to three.

"My wife and kids are still in London right now," he noted. "They get back on Friday so I haven't actually seen my kids since I won. I spoke to them, obviously, on FaceTime and stuff so I'm excited to see them and show them the trophy. I know they'll be trying to play with it and pick it up and it's quite heavy and so I might have to keep an eye on it this time but normally, the two boys, especially, just smash the ball around and then whoever wins picks up the trophy that I bring home but I'll have to explain it's a little bit more precious, so we'll have to keep an eye on it."
